tldr: To break through the voltage limitation (48 V or lower) of commercial drivers, the researchers developed "LunaDrive," an ultra-thin 70 mm diameter, 96 V-class motor driver using GaN FETs, achieving stable operation at an ultra-high electrical frequency of 3110 Hz through control delay compensation.
hero_caption: External view of LunaDrive and the high-speed load lifting experiment driven by high voltage. Despite its circular 70 mm diameter form factor that fits on the rear side of a flat BLDC motor, 100 V operation enables dynamic load lifting performance.
overview:
Dynamic robot motions such as backflips in humanoids and quadrupedal robots require high-power flat brushless DC (BLDC) motors that can generate massive instantaneous power. However, many commercially available servo motors and drivers are constrained to operating voltages of 48 V or lower. This "velocity saturation," where motor rotational speed tops out, has been a major bottleneck limiting dynamic performance. Because maximum rotational speed is proportional to applied voltage, driving motors beyond their rated voltage is desirable. Nevertheless, conventional Si MOSFETs suffer from a severe trade-off between voltage rating and current capacity, making it difficult to achieve both high voltage and high current in a size compact enough to mount on the rear of a small motor.

To address this, the authors turned to GaN FETs (gallium nitride field-effect transistors), a next-generation power semiconductor. They designed "LunaDrive," a motor driver that packs GaN FET half-bridge circuits and an optimized array of high-capacitance capacitors onto an ultra-thin circular board measuring only 8.51 mm thick and 70 mm in diameter. Furthermore, driving a high-pole-count motor (21 pole pairs) at high speeds under high voltage causes electrical frequencies to surge to around 3000 Hz, introducing a new challenge: control system delays lead to diverging instability. The authors tamed this ultra-high-frequency operation by implementing precision delay compensation within both the encoder and the microcontroller.

In experiments under 96 V operation, LunaDrive achieved stable rotation at an electrical frequency of 3110 Hz (mechanical speed of 8890 rpm) and proved that compensation is indispensable, as omitting it caused immediate diverging oscillations and shutdowns. The driver also demonstrated overwhelming current capacity—30 A continuous with a heat sink and an 80 A peak even without one. Finally, a high-speed wire-lifting experiment of an 8.1 kg load driven by a 24S LiPo battery (100 V) demonstrated practical performance directly applicable to dynamic behaviors like jumping.
contributions: Designed and fabricated "LunaDrive," an ultra-thin GaN FET motor driver with a diameter of 70 mm and a thickness of 8.51 mm, capable of direct mounting on the rear side of flat BLDC motors.

Demonstrated control stabilization under ultra-high electrical frequencies exceeding 3000 Hz resulting from high-voltage multi-pole flat motor drive, achieved through dual delay compensation in both the encoder and microcontroller.
Proposed an area efficiency evaluation method for multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) considering DC-bias characteristics, securing sufficient effective capacitance in constrained spaces.
Achieved 30 A continuous and 80 A peak current under 96 V operation, and demonstrated significant mitigation of velocity saturation in a 100 V battery-driven high-speed lifting test.

sections.heading: Why are high-voltage drive and GaN necessary?
sections.summary: Dynamic robot motions demand high speed and high torque, but existing drivers predominantly run at 48 V and face speed limits. Replacing Si with GaN FETs is effective, yet drivers fitting on the rear side of compact robotic motors were virtually non-existent. Furthermore, high-voltage drive of multi-pole motors pushes electrical frequencies to several kHz, making control delay compensation inevitable.
sections.details:
In recent years, humanoids and quadrupedal robots performing backflips have increasingly emerged. Powering these systems are "flat BLDC motors" capable of generating large torque with low gear ratios. Integrated servo motors combining reducers and drivers have also become popular, but most commercial products limit rated voltages to 48 V or lower. Because motor rotational speed is proportional to applied voltage, this 48 V barrier caps maximum operating velocity, impeding instantaneous dynamic movements.

While raising the voltage is the obvious solution, conventional silicon (Si) MOSFETs have a physical trade-off: higher breakdown voltage increases on-resistance, preventing large current flow. GaN FETs emerge as the prime candidate, combining high voltage ratings with low on-resistance in miniature packages. Although extensively studied in power electronics, conventional prototype circuits were large, heavy testbench setups; no thin, lightweight drivers existed that could be embedded on the rear side of dynamic robot joint motors.

Beyond hardware, software hurdles are equally severe. The target flat BLDC motor features a high pole pair count of $p=21$. Because electrical angular velocity in motor control is $p$ times the mechanical velocity, spinning the motor at high voltages causes the electrical frequency to reach roughly 3000 Hz. Standard commercial BLDC drivers recommend limits around 700 Hz, meaning this enters an operating region more than four times higher. In such ultra-high-speed regimes, tiny delays in microcontroller computations and encoder communications cause fatal phase shifts, leading to torque reduction and control divergence. Therefore, this study tackles both the hardware design of the compact GaN "LunaDrive" and delay compensation control to overcome this ultra-high-frequency realm.

captions.F2: Board configuration (top and bottom views) of the developed LunaDrive. It features a two-layer stacked structure with the controller board on the left and the driver board on the right, electrically isolating the logic power and motor power domains.

sections.heading: Circuit and control innovations packing massive power into an ultra-compact footprint
sections.summary: LunaDrive employs a two-board stack (70 mm diameter, 8.51 mm thickness) utilizing 150 V rated GaN FETs. Key designs include an area-optimized capacitor selection strategy, delay-compensated FOC within both the encoder and MCU, and a dedicated wire-winding module with copper heat sinks.
sections.details:
### II-A Hardware Design of the GaN FET Motor Driver
LunaDrive fits closely onto the rear of a flat motor with a 70 mm diameter and 8.51 mm thickness. It uses a two-board stacked architecture:
- **Controller Board**: Houses CAN FD for host communication, a magnetic encoder, and a control microcontroller (Microchip PIC32MK). Logic power (12 V) and motor power (96 V) are completely separated via digital isolators to enhance noise immunity.
- **Driver Board**: Arranges a 3-phase GaN FET half-bridge. To conduct high currents, an 8-layer board with 2 oz copper foil (equivalent to 16 oz total) was adopted. The switching devices are EPC2305 with a 150 V rating and 3 mΩ on-resistance. While GaN FETs switch rapidly, their reverse conduction loss during dead time is significant. To prioritize stability against abrupt motor load variations, a relatively long dead time of 100 ns was deliberately set, with parallel Schottky barrier diodes (SBDs) connected to curb losses. Additionally, because the gate voltage tolerance is 6 V with only a 1 V margin, dedicated gate driver ICs with built-in LDOs were placed, keeping gate traces under 5 mm.
- **Capacitor Layout Strategy**: Bulk capacitors for power supply smoothing represent a major challenge on compact boards. Multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) suffer from sharp drops in effective capacitance under DC-bias voltages. The authors evaluated capacitors using an effective capacitance per unit area index, $C_{\mathrm{area}}$. As a result, they determined that placing two 100 V rated components in series achieves higher area efficiency under DC bias than placing a single 250 V rated component. Within a 4 mm board height limit, a total of 106 capacitors were packed like a puzzle.

### II-B Field-Oriented Control (FOC) Incorporating Delay Compensation
Standard Field-Oriented Control (FOC) is utilized, but when electrical angular velocity $\omega_e$ becomes huge, the estimated electrical angle error $\omega_e T_d$ caused by system delay time $T_d$ can no longer be ignored. Delays stem primarily from three sources: internal encoder delay, microcontroller computation delay, and post-gate-drive delays. In this work, internal sensor delay is compensated using an ams OSRAM AS5147U encoder equipped with Dynamic Angle Error Compensation (DAEC). For delays occurring from the MCU onward, an algorithm was introduced to additively advance the electrical angle forward within the FOC control loop (25 kHz).

### II-C Wire-Winding Module and Thermal Design
For evaluation, an ultra-compact wire module incorporating a CubeMars RO80 frameless flat BLDC motor (21 pole pairs) was fabricated. High-strength wire (Dyneema/Zylon type) is wound around a 10 mm radius pulley. For GaN FET thermal management, two types of copper heat sinks were prepared: a "flat heat sink (15 mm thickness)" milled from copper parts and 1 mm copper plate, and a "finned heat sink (17.8 mm thickness)" equipped with 24 small fins.

captions.F7: CAD assembly view of the high-power wire-winding module incorporating LunaDrive. LunaDrive is directly coupled to the rear of the RO80 frameless BLDC motor, driving the wire at high speeds via a pulley.

sections.heading: Entering the >3000 Hz electrical frequency realm with massive current capability
sections.summary: After validating switching waveforms, maximum rotational speed was compared with and without delay compensation under 96 V drive, achieving 8890 rpm (3110 Hz electrical frequency) with compensation. Furthermore, 30 A continuous and 80 A peak current capabilities were confirmed, and an 8.1 kg weight-lifting experiment using a 100 V battery demonstrated high instantaneous power overcoming velocity saturation.
sections.details:
### III-A Switching Waveform Measurements
First, drain-to-source voltages of the GaN FETs were verified on an oscilloscope under 10 A motor current. The slew rate was set to 4.5 V/ns as a safety margin for noise reduction. Overshoot and ringing were extremely small, confirming stable switching behavior.

### III-B High-Speed Rotation Experiments via Delay Compensation
Supply voltage was raised from conventional 48 V to 96 V, and maximum rotational speed was measured with a 5 A current command under no load.
- **At 48 V**: Speed saturated at 4340 rpm regardless of delay compensation.
- **At 96 V without Delay Compensation**: The moment speed reached 5760 rpm, control delays caused coupling between d- and q-axes, triggering diverging oscillations in current waveforms and halting operation via overcurrent protection.
- **At 96 V with Delay Compensation**: The motor accelerated smoothly up to 8890 rpm without any divergence. The electrical frequency reached an astonishing 3110 Hz. This clearly demonstrated that delay compensation plays a decisive role in stabilizing control in high-speed regions.

### III-C Current Capability Validation on Target Motor (RO80)
The ability to deliver instantaneous maximum torque was tested on the RO80 embedded in the wire module. Applying current up to 60 A, the measured wire tension easily exceeded 400 N (the tension converted from peak motor torque specifications). Additionally, under the most severe thermal condition—locking the electrical angle and driving continuous 20 A through a single phase—the motor temperature reached its limit (80 °C) before the driver board did, with the board staying 6.5 °C cooler. This proves the board is not the thermal bottleneck.

### III-D Standalone Driver Limit Performance Evaluation
A larger drone motor was used as a load to probe the driver's limits.
- **Peak Current**: Even without a heat sink, LunaDrive stably supplied 80 A of current for 0.5 s.
- **Continuous Current (10 min run to 80 °C limit)**: Reached 13 A without a heat sink, 28 A with the flat heat sink, and 30 A with the finned heat sink. Note that without a heat sink, idling at 0 A switching caused the board temperature to rise to 46.8 °C, exhibiting the impact of GaN parasitic capacitance charging/discharging losses under 96 V operation.

### III-E High-Speed Load Lifting Experiment Mimicking Dynamic Robots
Assuming a jumping robot, an experiment lifting an 8.1 kg load over 0.5 m with a wire was conducted using a LiPo 24S (100 V) power source. Under 50 V drive, velocity saturation occurred in the late acceleration phase, failing to maintain the 50 A command current. Under 100 V drive, the full 50 A was sustained almost until the end of the stroke. Maximum lifting velocity increased by approximately 19%, from 4.14 m/s to 4.92 m/s, demonstrating explosive instantaneous power that slammed into the upper bumper cushion.

captions.F10: Current and motor speed responses under 96 V drive. On the left without delay compensation, diverging oscillations cause a shutdown near 5760 rpm; on the right with delay compensation, rotation remains stable up to 8890 rpm (equivalent to 3110 Hz).
captions.F12: Temperature evolution during continuous 20 A conduction into the RO80 motor. The motor reached its 80 °C limit first, while the driver board remained 6.5 °C cooler, demonstrating thermal headroom in the driver.

sections.heading: Unprecedented power density compared to premier commercial drivers
sections.summary: LunaDrive was compared against Elmo's Gold Solo Twitter, a benchmark compact high-power driver. In thickness-constrained robot joint spaces, LunaDrive delivers higher continuous and peak current densities even without a heat sink than the Elmo driver does with one, highlighting the advantages of GaN FETs.
sections.details:
To clarify LunaDrive's performance standing, it was compared with Elmo Motion Control's "Gold Solo Twitter," an ultra-compact high-power driver widely used in robotics.

In robotic actuator design, minimizing "thickness" is paramount to avoid joint protrusions. Elmo's 100 V-class driver measures 19.35 mm thick; under 85 V operation, its continuous current is 3 A without a heat sink and 12 A with a finned heat sink (28.85 mm thick), with a peak current of 45 A. Furthermore, this does not include an onboard encoder, adding extra thickness when integrated into an actuator.

In contrast, LunaDrive measures just 8.51 mm thick while incorporating an onboard magnetic encoder. It delivers 13 A continuous without a heat sink, 30 A continuous with a 17.8 mm finned heat sink, and an 80 A peak current. Although heat sink conditions and conduction paths differ, preventing an exact 1-to-1 comparison, LunaDrive's bare-board continuous current density surpasses Elmo's driver equipped with a large heat sink. Combining 150 V rated GaN FETs, an optimized MLCC layout, and an ultra-thick copper multi-layer PCB pushes robotic driver power density to an entirely new level.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: By fusing GaN FETs with delay compensation, LunaDrive proves that high-voltage, high-current drive of flat BLDC motors is feasible in an ultra-thin form factor. Future work will integrate this system into actual robots to dramatically boost dynamic jumping and agile maneuvers.
sections.details:
This paper presented and validated "LunaDrive," an ultra-compact motor driver capable of driving flat BLDC motors far beyond their rated voltages to advance dynamic robot performance.

Within a disc shape of 70 mm diameter and 8.51 mm thickness, it integrates GaN FET half-bridges, a 106-capacitor array maximizing effective capacitance, and an isolated controller. In the challenging regime exceeding 3000 Hz electrical frequency under 96 V+ voltages, delay compensation in both sensor and MCU prevented divergence and achieved stable rotation at 8890 rpm. The driver also logged 30 A continuous and 80 A peak current, demonstrating the ability to overcome velocity saturation.

Future work aims to move beyond standalone benchmarks by integrating LunaDrive into full robot platforms, such as humanoid or jumping robot leg mechanisms, to validate system-level dynamic performance improvements.

takeaways: When driving motors at high voltages exceeding ratings, control delay becomes the dominant instability factor as electrical frequency rises, making proactive compensation in both encoder and MCU essential.
For bulk capacitors on compact high-voltage boards, using effective capacitance per unit area—factoring in DC-bias degradation—dramatically optimizes layout efficiency.
Adopting GaN FETs enables more than double the peak current (80 A) and superior power density compared to premier commercial Si drivers (like Elmo), all within an 8.5 mm thickness.
Raising driver operating voltage (from 48 V to 96 V / 100 V) rather than staying constrained by nominal motor ratings significantly pushes back velocity saturation limits during dynamic motions.
limitations: Under high-voltage (96 V) operation, switching losses from parasitic capacitance charging and discharging are substantial, causing the board to self-heat to approximately 47 °C even at 0 A idle.
During instantaneous high-current surges up to 80 A, thermal response lag in the board thermistor prevents accurate real-time monitoring of GaN FET junction temperatures.
In the lifting experiment, the acceleration stroke was limited to 0.5 m, capping the maximum velocity improvement at roughly 19% under 100 V operation.
